name: Video and UGC ad scripts (hooks, first 3 seconds, shoot plans)
asked_as: a Reels ad for our new product
new hooks for our video ads
our video ads lose people in the first few seconds
outcome: Scripts the owner, a customer or a creator can film on a phone without a call: each with at least three openers to test, timed beats with the exact spoken lines and on-screen text, a shot list that fits who and what is really available, the one claim it rests on with its proof, and the number that will say it worked.
first_principles: The first 3 seconds are the ad: most viewers leave during the hook. Write the opener as three levers (what is seen, what is said, the words on screen) and test 3 to 5 openers on one body before writing new bodies.

A hook must filter, not just stop. Delivery learns from who keeps watching, so a broad curiosity or meme hook trains the ad toward people who never buy. Name the buyer, their moment or their problem in the first line.
Many people watch with the sound off. The words on screen must make the point on their own; the spoken line and the on-screen line say the same thing in different words.

Who can be on camera picks the format, not the other way round: a founder with a true story, real customers with consent, a creator who has used the product for weeks, or hands and product only. Never an AI-made person presented as a customer.

Show, don't claim. The body shows the product doing its job (the texture, the fit, the size in hand, the box as it arrives) and holds one claim with its proof; feature lists lose the second half. In problem-led ads the product comes in late; in demos it is there from the first frame.
Read by the second: hook rate (3-second views over impressions) judges the opener, hold rate judges the body, store-side cost per purchase judges the ad. Fix the part that leaks and keep what holds.

look_for: Opener or body: a high hook rate with a steep drop before the product means the body loses them (often the jump from hook to pitch); a low hook rate on a body that holds the people who stay means the body deserves new openers, not a rewrite.
A hook that stops but does not filter: hook rate well above the account's, purchases well below. The opener needs the buyer, their moment or their problem named.

The product too early or too late: on a cold problem-led ad the product in second 1 reads as an ad and people swipe; in a demo, a product that appears at second 15 loses everyone who wanted to see it work.
Lines nobody would say: brochure copy read to camera. Spoken lines come from reviews and comments, in the buyer's own words, under about 12 words each.
A failed sound-off test: muted, the first 3 seconds do not say who it is for or what it does.
One face, one room: every video uses the same person in the same setting. A new presenter or place on a proven script can revive spend; recut footage of the same person often cannot.
A long-running winner whose openers were never tested: 3 to 5 new openers on its body is the cheapest win in the account.
Hidden words: captions, price or product under the platform's buttons and caption area (the bottom third and the right edge).
Claims said aloud that the page or proof cannot back: results in a set time, 'clinically', 'best', 'safe for everyone'.
Formats never tried: founder to camera, a customer review, day in the life, unboxing, a 15-second demo, a reply to a comment. Rivals running one of these for months is a strong hint.

decisions.recommend: Pick from the diagnosis: trust gap, founder or review; 'does it work', demo; 'what will arrive' or gifting, unboxing; 'will it fit my life', day in the life. If one format has clearly won in data/creatives.md, lead with it and add one new format as the test.

rules: Each script names its hypothesis at the top: one buyer in one moment, one want, one claim with its proof.
Pick the format from formats.json by insight_fit and by who can really be on camera; high-effort formats only when the people, footage or budget exist.
The first 3 seconds are written on all three levers (the visual, the spoken line, the on-screen text), with at least 3 openers per body, each a different tactic.
Spoken lines are read aloud before hand-over: about 2.5 words a second, each line under about 12 words, in buyer words from reviews and comments.
On-screen text makes the point with the sound off and sits inside the safe zone (keep about 14% of the top, 35% of the bottom and 6% of each side clear on 9:16).
Every shot is one the presenter can get in the stated place, with the stated kit, in the stated time; the product is shown exactly as it ships.
A creator says only what they experienced: experience lines are prompts to answer in their own words, and they have used the product long enough to say them.
Paid use is agreed in writing before filming; a paid creator's ad says so on screen and aloud, early in the video (ASCI in India, FTC in the US).
Never an AI-made person presented as a customer, reviewer or founder; AI-made clips carry the platform's AI label.
Two cuts per body (about 15 and 30 seconds); length comes from the body, never from padding.
The call to action is spoken and on screen, and matches the first screen of the page it points to.
When the owner gives no count, 5 or 6 scripts across at least 3 formats, each with 3 openers and two cuts; every chosen hypothesis gets at least two formats.
Every script ships with its post copy: primary text with the hook in the first 125 characters, a headline under 40 characters and the call to action, in the brand's words, checked with copy-check.
Every script has a 9:16 cut for Reels and Stories and a 4:5 cut for feed, with the safe zones and where the product sits in each.
Personas are named only with the one line that says who they are and the number behind them.
